title: Deutsche Bank's Private Bank selects Thought Machine for radical core banking shakeup
summary:
Deutsche Bank’s Private Bank has reached an important milestone in the multi-year transformation of its technology infrastructure, advancing the strategic priorities announced at the end of 2025 as part of Deutsche Bank’s new strategic cycle which runs until the end of 2028. At that time, the bank announced plans to simplify the Private Bank’s global banking landscape by reducing the number of core banking systems from 15 to two modern, cloud-based platforms. The first of these two platforms has now been selected.
To support this transformation, Deutsche Bank’s Private Bank has selected Vault Core, the cloud-native core banking platform developed by financial technology company Thought Machine. It will serve as the core banking engine for all banking and lending products in Germany across both Personal Banking and Wealth Management. The platform will be used to modernise the bank’s technology foundation, allowing Deutsche Bank to replace fragmented legacy systems, reduce complexity, and accelerate time-to-market for new products through a more client-centric operating model. It will support the Private Bank's strategic objectives of driving operating leverage in Personal Banking while providing a scalable platform to support continued growth in Wealth Management.
Yiping Li, Chief Operating Officer of Deutsche Bank’s Private Bank, said:
“With the selection of our future core banking platform, we are now turning strategy into execution. Modernising our core banking infrastructure will help us simplify our technology landscape, reduce complexity and create a more scalable foundation for future growth. Ultimately, this transformation is about delivering a better experience for clients and employees while strengthening the foundations of our business for the years ahead.”
Development work is already underway, with testing planned as one of the key milestones towards year-end. The migration will then be carried out in phases, with existing systems and the new platform operating in parallel throughout the transition period. Products will be migrated progressively from 2027 onwards, supporting a controlled and stable migration while ensuring operational resilience and continuity of service.
Christian Rhino, Chief Information Officer of Deutsche Bank’s Private Bank, said:
“Modernising our core banking landscape is one of the most significant technology transformations currently underway in the Private Bank. Vault Core provides a modern, cloud-native foundation that enhances resilience, scalability and flexibility. By separating product logic from underlying infrastructure, we will be able to develop, adapt and deploy products more efficiently over time, while progressively reducing reliance on fragmented legacy systems.”
Paul Taylor, CEO and founder of Thought Machine, said:
"Deutsche Bank is setting a clear precedent for how major international banks can modernise their core infrastructure. Replacing disjointed legacy systems with a modern architecture gives the bank the real-time capability needed to streamline operations, strengthen system reliability, and deliver superior customer experiences at scale. We are delighted to enter into this decade-long partnership."
For the implementation of the platform, Deutsche Bank has selected GFT as transformation and system integration partner for Vault Core, leveraging GFT's extensive experience as a delivery partner for Thought Machine implementations worldwide.
Christopher Ortiz, Group Executive Board Member and Chief Executive Global Accounts & Offerings, GFT Technologies:
“Modernizing core banking is a foundational step in any bank's technology transformation. Together with Deutsche Bank and Thought Machine, we are helping build a modern, scalable platform that supports innovation, operational efficiency and future growth, while creating the technology foundation to harness the potential of AI.”
As part of its multi-year transformation, Deutsche Bank’s Private Bank plans to invest around EUR 600 million in IT, operations and artificial intelligence by the end of 2028. The programme is expected to deliver annual run-rate savings of around EUR 300 million by 2028 while simplifying and modernising the bank’s technology landscape.

We welcome today’s announcement, which will further boost our work to support innovation in financial services without compromising on financial stability.

title: Aussie fintechs Lucie Money taps Fiskil to embed open banking data into its conversational AI agent
summary:
Lucie Money, the Sydney fintech building a conversational money agent, has gone live under Australia’s Consumer Data Right (CDR) by leveraging Fiskil’s infrastructure to securely access open banking data. 
With customer consent, Lucie Money will import banking transaction data directly into the app - privately and securely – using Fiskil's advanced infrastructure.
Lucie Money is building on open banking, to avoid manual uploads and screen scraping, so customers can have confidence that trusted bank data is being used to deliver reliable answers to money questions. 
Anthony Voigt, Founder & CEO of Lucie Money, said: “Lucie Money starts with bank data, collected securely and categorised properly. Then it helps with budgets and goals, and knowing whether you'll get there. You can't do any of that without accurate data underneath it."
Using the app's conversational interface, customers can ask what they can afford, whether a bill is covered, or where their spending has drifted since last month. 
The AI-enabled agent answers those questions directly and in plain language, so the customer does not have to try to interpret a dashboard.
“Most people are doing their best with their money and still aren't sure it's enough," Voigt said.
"That's the gap I want Lucie Money to close," he emphasised. "You don't have to do all this yourself; you have an agent by your side.”
The app delivers the power of AI without putting users at risk by entering sensitive information into a publicly available LLM. 
"Lucie Money keeps an eye on your money, tells you when something needs attention and helps you get things done, rather than waiting to be asked," Voigt added. 
“Lucie Money can help with a funding plan for a big one-off expense like an overseas holiday, by surfacing the available options and communicating the financial tradeoffs. You could chat through what a regular weekly savings goal would look like in the time available, or what it would mean to tap into emergency money,” Voigt said.
As Lucie Money’s CDR principal, Fiskil will enable the critical integration that will connect Lucie Money’s customers with their personal financial data via open banking.
Under the arrangement, Fiskil holds the CDR accreditation and Lucie Money operates as its CDR representative, bound by the CDR obligations passed through in that agreement. 
“Fiskil is delighted to support Lucie Money’s open banking data feeds as their chosen infrastructure provider,” said Jacob Parker, CEO & Founder of Fiskil.
“The benefits of open banking for Lucie Money’s customers include real-time bank data sync, enhanced security, time efficiency and personal insights,” Parker added.
"This is an exciting first step for Lucie Money because nothing we build later will work unless the architecture is right in the first place," Voigt noted.

title: NMI Research: Consumers Want AI to Help Them Shop, Not Control Their Spending
summary:
The technology industry is racing towards AI agents that can browse, choose and buy on a consumer’s behalf, but American shoppers are not there yet. They want AI to help them find products, save money and remove friction from checkout, but they still want a human hand on the final purchase. New research from NMI®, a global leader in embedded payments infrastructure, reveals a significant gap between the industry hype surrounding agentic commerce and the authority consumers are currently prepared to give AI.
NMI’s Embedded Payments: Agentic Commerce Reality Check, a survey of 1,000 U.S. adults, found that consumers are increasingly using AI to start their shopping journeys, but few are ready to let it finish the job. While Salesforce reports a 200% rise in consumers using AI as their first step in shopping, NMI found that just 11% have used it to complete a transaction.
Consumers are embracing AI as a shopping assistant, using it to find information, discover products and save money, but most are not ready to let it make the final decision or spend on their behalf:
Just 10% would give AI full control over a purchase
45% would not trust AI to make purchases on their behalf at all
70% say they must be able to review or override AI’s decision before a purchase is made
69% do not trust AI to process payments securely
Tiffany Johnson, Chief Product Officer at NMI, said:


Consumers want AI to remove friction, not remove their involvement

The research shows that consumers are not rejecting AI in commerce. Instead, they are drawing a clear boundary between tasks that assist them and decisions that commit their money.
63% would use AI to insert discount codes automatically during checkout
59% are comfortable with AI recommending products
58% would allow AI to fill in their shipping address
57% believe AI can make shopping faster and more convenient
56% would use it to make checkout faster and more seamless
That willingness declines sharply as AI begins to make more personal or consequential decisions. Fifty-eight percent (58%) are uncomfortable with AI recommending clothing sizes based on customer reviews, while 55% do not want AI recommending which payment method they should use. Seventy-six percent (76%) are uncomfortable with AI completing purchases on their behalf, and only 3% currently describe AI as a personal shopper that manages every stage of the shopping journey.
Parents and younger consumers are moving faster, but still want boundaries

Similarly, 48% of both Millennials and Gen Z say they are excited about agentic commerce and believe it could make their lives easier. But even among these earlier adopters, relatively few are prepared to hand over complete purchasing authority. Only 14% of Millennials and 13% of Gen Z would give AI full control over a purchase.
The findings suggest that greater familiarity with AI increases enthusiasm for agentic commerce, but does not remove the need for strong safeguards.
Trust, control and transparency will determine adoption

Trust: consumers need confidence that their money and payment information will remain secure:
69% do not trust AI to process payments securely
61% cite security or fraud as a concern about AI completing purchases
84% have never uploaded payment details to an AI tool to enable purchases
The consequences of a failure would extend beyond the company providing the AI. If an AI tool made a purchase before a consumer was ready, 62% would blame the AI provider, but 34% would blame the retailer and nearly one in four, 24%, would hold the payments provider responsible.
Control: consumers want to set clear boundaries around what an AI agent is permitted to do:
70% say it is important that they can review or override an AI decision before a purchase
60% worry AI could spend more than they intended
57% are concerned about losing control over purchases
Transparency: consumers also want to understand what AI has selected and why before their money moves:
58% worry an AI shopping agent could purchase the wrong item, size, color or brand
50% are concerned about having limited visibility into AI’s decisions
55% do not want AI recommending their payment method

title: Multiplier Raises $6M Seed Financing to Build AI for Asset Managers
summary:
Multiplier, an AI company making agent harnesses for asset managers, has raised a $6 million seed financing round. The round was led by Lux Capital with participation from Y Combinator, GoAhead Ventures, Rebel Fund, General Advance, Unpopular Ventures, and Amino Capital. Additional investors include Greg Jensen and Karen Karniol-Tambour (co-CIOs, Bridgewater Associates), Pete Briger (Chairman, Fortress Investment Group), Jasjeet Sekhon (CSO, DeepMind), Sandeep Nailwal (CEO, Polygon), Kaz Nejatian (CEO, OpenDoor), and Multiplier customers (especially Mercator Partners).
“We tried nearly every tool on the market and ended up with an unwieldy collection of fragmented point solutions,” said Michael Siliciano, co-founder of California hedge fund Verso Partners. “We’ve also attempted to build our own tools, but maintaining them became a full-time job. That’s why we brought in Multiplier.”
Multiplier is the via media between hobbled software and duct-taped DIY AI efforts for leading asset management firms.
“Early vertical tools have grown fast,” said Ian McInnis, Multiplier’s co-founder and CEO. “‘ChatGPT, but for finance, and it has some data access, and it’s compliant.’ Okay, great.” Architectural and product decisions that helped others move faster have left investment management firms unprepared for the agentic era.
“You still need domain specialization, but you also need firm specialization,” said McInnis. “Your data access demands are now ‘all the data, information, and context that I as a human can access and then some,’ whether or not the providers have built nice MCPs. Now that the AI’s getting woven so deeply into your firm, your security demands go way beyond compliance box-ticking. Investors are legitimately concerned about their edge being stolen. All these demands are difficult to satisfy on webapps.”
Multiplier meets those demands with repeatable infrastructure: it deploys the same substrate inside each customer’s own systems, then builds firm-specific customizations on top. Every firm needs that substrate, but frameworks, info sources, processes, and tastes necessarily differ, so Multiplier builds bespoke evals for each firm it works with. “For the time being, that’s what it takes,” said McInnis. “Without evals, your AI drifts whenever you try to do any kind of continual learning, gets kind of crufty and dumb. It slips back into pretraining biases. Those biases are also why you need investor oversight when building evals.”
McInnis was an investor at Bridgewater Associates until February, and COO Ryan Winkler left StepStone Group in April. CTO/President Ben Finch–––formerly founding researcher at AI unicorn Sentient Labs–––brought the group together at Princeton University to start a student-run hedge fund, which has beaten the S&P 500 every year.
Users spend many hours daily in the product, which expedites everything from top-of-funnel idea generation to post-trade review. “The most valuable dataset inside an asset manager is not the market data everyone can buy, but the firm’s accumulated research, judgment, and decision history,” said Phil Brady of GoAhead Ventures. “Multiplier provides the missing connective tissue.”
Long/short investment manager Mercator Partners helped to incubate Multiplier, betting on the team before a product existed. Martin Fransson, head of primary research at Mercator Partners, described Multiplier as “a tremendous internal proprietary knowledge flywheel.” Scott Hobart, CIO of Mercator Partners, said, “We used to spend 80% of our time gathering information and 20% acting on it. Multiplier has flipped those percentages.”

title: Fiat Republic and ClearBank Partner to Support MiCA Safeguarding for European Digital Asset Platforms
summary:
Fiat Republic, the regulated B2B fiat infrastructure for crypto, today announced a channel partnership with ClearBank, the enabler of real-time clearing and embedded banking, that will allow European crypto asset service providers (CASPs) to meet their MiCA safeguarding obligations without leaving the Fiat Republic environment.
Under MiCA, many digital asset companies are required to hold client funds in a segregated account at a licensed credit institution - separate from operational funds. Until now, platforms using Fiat Republic for day-to-day transactional banking and virtual account reconciliation were required to manually sweep client funds to an external bank each evening and return them the following morning, creating significant operational friction and compliance overhead.
The new partnership removes that requirement entirely. ClearBank, authorised by the European Central Bank and supervised by De Nederlandsche Bank, provides the regulated credit institution infrastructure. Fiat Republic acts as channel partner, meaning clients retain their existing technical, commercial and legal relationship with Fiat Republic while gaining direct access to ClearBank-backed safeguarding accounts. This means no multiple contact points for the combined service or daily sweeps.
Adam Bialy, Founder and CEO, Fiat Republic, commented, "MiCA created a compliance requirement that was forcing our clients to maintain two separate banking relationships just to keep operating. That's unnecessary friction in an already complex regulatory environment. This partnership with ClearBank means our clients can meet their safeguarding obligations through the same infrastructure they already use for transactional banking - and focus on growing their business instead of managing cash movements overnight."
Tristan Kirchner, CEO of ClearBank Europe, adds," MiCA has fundamentally changed what European crypto platforms need from their banking partners. For any platform seeking or holding a MiCA licence, regulated safeguarding is now a hard regulatory requirement. Building this solution with Fiat Republic was a natural extension of our existing relationship and ensures their clients can meet those obligations without the operational complexity of managing multiple banking arrangements. We're pleased to provide the regulated banking infrastructure that helps make that possible."
The partnership is available immediately to MiCA-licensed digital asset companies and those currently in the application process, subject to eligibility.
This announcement follows Fiat Republic's launch earlier this year as the first live client on ClearBank's SEPA Indirect product, which gave clients in France access to virtual IBANs and euro payments under their own BICs.
